newsitem.title: DUBAI: FOCUS-Iraq eases back into oil market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Iraq eases back into oil market.

text.p: Iraq, ostracised by world oil markets since its invasion of Kuwait six years ago, has found little difficulty in enticing foreign oil firms to rekindle old ties, Gulf-based Western traders said on Monday.

"It's been a long wait. Now it's finally over...Iraq is back as a marketing force," said a Gulf trader when Iraqi oil exports flowed back onto international markets under a strictly monitored United Nations oil-for-food plan.
Iraq's petroleum exports had been restricted to limited sales to Jordan and by large-scale smuggling by road tankers through Turkey and by ships through Gulf waters.

Iraqi Oil Minister Muhammad Rasheed said on Sunday that Iraq had signed oil contracts with 11 foreign firms including some in the United States, which led the allied effort which ejected Iraqi forces from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.
The first oil to flow out was on a tanker carrying 153,500 tonnes of Iraq's Kirkuk crude which left the Turkish Mediterranean port of Ceyhan on Monday.

Washington has given its approval for U.S. Coastal Corp to buy 60,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Iraqi Basrah crude which traders expect Coastal will take to its refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba.

Coastal's hired tanker Star of Africa was being loaded on Monday with two million barrels of Iraqi crude at the Mina al-Bakr offshore oil terminal in the northern Gulf, 12 miles (19 km) off the southern Fao Peninsula.
Alongside Coastal's vessel was a tanker chartered by U.S. independent oil firm Bayoil, Gulf sources said.

Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) has been quick to tie up contracts to meet the U.N. deal under which Iraq is allowed to export $2 billion of its oil on a renewal basis every six months.
At current prices this equates to between 500,000 and 600,000 bpd of crude -- more than the entire oil output of Australia but less than one percent of total world supply.

Wider sanctions against Iraq which would allow the country to export unrestricted amounts of oil are still in place and will not be removed until U.N. inspectors are satisfied that thay can account for all of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

Oil deals have already been struck by SOMO with Turkey's state refiner TUPRAS, France's Total SA, Japan's Mitsubishi Corp, and Italy's Oil Energy while negotiations are continiung with a range of other companies from Europe, Japan, South America and the United States.
A Total spokesman on Monday that the Paris-based firm had signed a contract with Iraq to take 30,000 bpd provided the United Nations approved the agreement.

Before its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait, Iraq was exporting 2.7 million bpd. Iraqi officials say the country now has an export capacity of two million bpd after restoring facilities which were targeted by allied bombing.
